cls: Conditionally essential amino acid / nitric oxide precursor (dietary supplement; IV form used diagnostically and as urea-cycle adjunct)
pharm: Amino acid - nitric oxide (NO) substrate, growth-hormone secretagogue, and ammonia-detoxification (urea cycle) intermediate
quick: Oral supplement commonly 2-6 g/day in divided doses (varies by use); IV (e.g., GH-stimulation test / urea-cycle adjunct) per protocol, typically 0.5 g/kg infused
Oral doses may be taken with or without food; splitting doses with meals may reduce GI upset
Limited data; dietary amounts considered low risk - use supplemental/high doses only if clearly indicated and supervised
Limited data; present naturally in milk - supplemental use should be supervised
Caution in renal impairment; IV arginine can cause hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis - reduce/avoid high doses
Caution in severe hepatic impairment; used as urea-cycle adjunct but high loads need monitoring
No specific interaction described; general moderation advised
Blood pressure, serum potassium and acid-base (IV), blood glucose; ammonia in urea-cycle use
summary: L-Arginine is a conditionally essential amino acid and the physiological substrate for nitric oxide synthase, making it a precursor of the vasodilator nitric oxide; it is also an intermediate in the hepatic urea cycle (ammonia detoxification) and stimulates secretion of growth hormone, insulin, and glucagon. It is marketed as an oral dietary supplement and is used in medicine intravenously as a provocative agent in growth-hormone stimulation testing and as an adjunct in certain urea-cycle disorders and severe hyperammonemia. IMPORTANT: as a supplement/amino acid it is NOT an FDA-approved drug; doses and indications are based on monographs and clinical literature rather than a single FDA label. Intravenous arginine hydrochloride can cause hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis and must be given with monitoring.
indications: Dietary supplementation as a conditionally essential amino acid / nitric oxide precursor (oral supplement use)
Provocative agent for growth-hormone (somatotropin) reserve testing (IV, under protocol)
Adjunct in the management of certain urea-cycle disorders and acute hyperammonemia (IV, specialist use)
Investigational/adjunctive uses (e.g., endothelial/vascular support, intermittent claudication, erectile function) - evidence variable and not FDA-approved

dosage.n: Doses and claims vary by product; supplement, not an approved drug indication

dosage.d: Arginine hydrochloride 0.5 g/kg (up to ~30 g) infused IV over ~30 minutes
dosage.n: Per endocrine testing protocol with serial GH sampling

dosage.d: Arginine hydrochloride 0.5 g/kg IV over ~30 minutes (max ~30 g)
dosage.n: Per protocol; monitor glucose and electrolytes

dosage.d: Specialist-directed IV arginine hydrochloride loading and maintenance per metabolic protocol
dosage.n: Dose depends on the specific enzyme defect; monitor ammonia, electrolytes, acid-base

admin: Oral supplement: take with or without food; dividing the daily amount across meals can reduce nausea, cramping, or diarrhea
IV arginine hydrochloride: dilute and infuse per protocol (e.g., GH testing over ~30 minutes) through a secure IV line; rapid infusion increases adverse effects
Monitor serum potassium and acid-base status with IV use - arginine hydrochloride delivers a chloride/acid load and can cause hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis
Use IV preparations only in monitored settings with access to glucose and electrolyte measurement (it stimulates insulin and can cause hypoglycemia)
Avoid extravasation of hypertonic IV solutions; follow the metabolic or endocrine team's protocol in urea-cycle use
moa: L-Arginine is a conditionally essential amino acid with several physiological roles. It is the sole substrate for the nitric oxide synthases, which convert it to nitric oxide (a potent endogenous vasodilator and signaling molecule) and citrulline; this underlies its proposed vascular/endothelial effects. Within hepatocytes it is a key intermediate of the urea cycle, where it is cleaved by arginase to urea and ornithine, providing a route for ammonia detoxification - the basis of its adjunctive use in urea-cycle disorders. Arginine also stimulates pancreatic islet secretion of insulin and glucagon and provokes pituitary release of growth hormone, the property exploited in growth-hormone stimulation testing. It additionally serves as a precursor for creatine, polyamines, proline, and agmatine.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to L-arginine or product components
Patients in whom a high acid/potassium/chloride load is dangerous should not receive IV arginine hydrochloride without correction (relative-to-absolute depending on severity)
relative: Renal impairment (risk of hyperkalemia and acidosis with IV use)
Recent myocardial infarction (caution - some data suggest harm with high-dose supplementation post-MI)
Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase / arginine-handling metabolic disorders; predisposition to hypotension
monitor: Blood glucose (insulin release - risk of hypoglycemia)

preg: Arginine is a naturally occurring amino acid present in the diet, and dietary amounts are considered low risk in pregnancy. Adequate and well-controlled data on high-dose or intravenous supplementation are limited; reserve supraphysiologic supplemental use for clear clinical indications under supervision.
lact: Arginine occurs naturally in human milk. There are limited data on the safety of high-dose supplementation during breastfeeding; supplemental use beyond dietary intake should be supervised.
renal: Use caution in renal impairment. Intravenous arginine hydrochloride delivers a substantial chloride/acid load and can precipitate hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis when renal excretion is reduced; lower the dose or avoid high-dose IV use and monitor potassium and acid-base status.
hepatic: Arginine is metabolized largely through the hepatic urea cycle. In severe hepatic impairment handling of an arginine/nitrogen load may be impaired; in urea-cycle disorders it is used therapeutically but only with close monitoring of ammonia, electrolytes, and acid-base balance.

moderate: Antihypertensives and nitrates/PDE-5 inhibitors (additive vasodilation/hypotension via the nitric oxide pathway)
Potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and potassium supplements (additive hyperkalemia risk with IV arginine hydrochloride)
minor: Antidiabetic agents (arginine stimulates insulin - theoretical additive glucose-lowering)
Sildenafil and similar agents (theoretical additive blood-pressure lowering)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; dividing doses with meals reduces gastrointestinal upset.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction described; general moderation advised.
interactions.diagnostics: Used itself as a provocative agent in growth-hormone testing; IV arginine can transiently alter potassium, glucose, and acid-base measurements.

serious: Hypotension (from nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation, especially IV)
Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis (IV arginine hydrochloride)
Hypoglycemia (insulin release, particularly with IV testing)
Worsened outcomes when used in high doses after acute myocardial infarction (reported in a clinical trial)
rare: Local infusion-site reactions with IV use

monitoring: Serum potassium and acid-base status with intravenous use
Blood glucose (risk of hypoglycemia from insulin stimulation)
Plasma ammonia and electrolytes when used in urea-cycle disorders
counsel: This is an amino acid sold as a dietary supplement; it is not an FDA-approved medicine - tell your clinician you are taking it
Take oral doses with food if it upsets your stomach, and split larger amounts through the day
It can lower blood pressure - be cautious if you take blood-pressure medicines, nitrates, or erectile-dysfunction drugs
If you have kidney or liver disease, or had a recent heart attack, check with your doctor before taking high doses
Stop and seek care if you feel faint, very dizzy, or have palpitations after dosing
pk: Oral: amino acid absorbed over minutes to hours; IV: physiological effects within minutes
Plasma peak roughly 1-2 hours after oral dosing; immediate with IV infusion
Short plasma half-life (on the order of ~1 hour); rapidly metabolized and incorporated
Effects are brief; sustained supplementation requires repeat/divided dosing
Store oral products at room temperature, tightly closed, away from moisture; store IV solutions per the manufacturer's labeling
pearls: DIETARY SUPPLEMENT / amino acid - NOT an FDA-approved drug; data drawn from monographs (e.g., BNF/EMA-type and clinical literature) rather than a single FDA label
Acts mainly as a nitric oxide precursor (vasodilation), a urea-cycle intermediate (ammonia handling), and a growth-hormone/insulin secretagogue
IV arginine is used as a provocative agent in growth-hormone stimulation testing - watch for hypoglycemia
IV arginine hydrochloride carries an acid/chloride load - risk of hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis, especially in renal impairment
A clinical trial found NO benefit and possible harm from high-dose arginine given after acute myocardial infarction - avoid in that setting
Can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect of nitrates, PDE-5 inhibitors, and antihypertensives
missed: If you miss a dose of an oral supplement, take it when you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume your usual schedule. Do not double up. Intravenous arginine is given as a one-time test or under a metabolic protocol rather than on a self-administered schedule.
overdose: Excessive intake, particularly intravenous, can cause gastrointestinal upset, hypotension, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypoglycemia. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive - stop the infusion, correct potassium and acid-base disturbances, treat hypoglycemia with glucose, and support blood pressure. Oral overdose typically causes self-limited gastrointestinal symptoms managed with hydration.
